26.t: No mixed bands: playing only with white bands until the Washingtonians
26.s: Greer says there were no mixed bands, that he never played a gig with a Black band before the Washingtonians, and credits Benny Goodman with presenting integrated groups.
26.q: I never in my life played with a colored band on a gig. Of course, I belonged to the Clef Club and I rehearsed with them, but on an actual gig, I never in my life played with no colored band till we had the Washingtonians.

26.t: Benny Goodman breaking the colour line
26.s: Greer credits Goodman with presenting Black musicians in his band, and with easing open the door.
26.q: No, no, no. It was a high honor because at this time the Iron Curtain was up, you know. I give Benny Goodman credit. He was the first one to break through when he got Hamp and Teddy ___. He was the first one to present the colored musicians with his band. Because before then it wasn't heard of.…

383.t: Racial mixing in the Goodman band compared with Jackie Robinson
383.s: Wilson says the band treated him like family, audiences were enthusiastic, and the experience was entirely different from Robinson's ten years later.
383.ch: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
383.q: Oh, it was a tremendous success. As a matter of fact, it was an asset, racial mixing. The interest in the United States was tremendous, and the public was so for the thing that not one negative voice in any audience did we ever get. Just tremendous enthusiasm. This interracial thing was just…

383.t: John Hammond's role in mixing studio bands and the Goodman Trio
383.s: Wilson credits Hammond with pressing Goodman to hire him publicly and with breaking the color line among radio staff musicians.
383.q: And I had played on records organized by Red Norvo; I made a lot of records with Krupa, with little groups^ Jack Teagarden and Charlie Teagarden and you probably did, too, all the mixed bands in those days did.

313.t: Racial mixing on records and Goodman integrating the stage
313.s: Black and white musicians seldom recorded together; Jelly Roll Morton, Condon, Waller, then Goodman, Wilson and Hampton broke the barrier.
313.q: Well there was in the sense that in the earlier days of jazz, black musicians and white musicians tended not to play together in public. And that included phonograph records for quite a while, although as we all know from the memoirs of everybody from

1034.t: John Hammond and integration of the Goodman band
1034.s: He knew John Hammond and tells how Hammond got Goodman to hire Teddy Wilson in 1935, and about earlier hidden integrated jamming.
1034.q: No. That’s what I talk about in my class and that’s where integration — when John Hammond, who I’m sure you know, knew, or know of — well I was lucky enough to know John Hammond. He worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. I worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. And I got to know Mr.…

440.t: Organizing the Goodman concert and bringing in Teddy Wilson for the trio
440.s: A union benefit concert sold out and made Time's cover; she then had Benny bring Teddy Wilson to form the first public interracial trio.
440.q: It was a concert that Stanley and I had heard. Except the thing was not known in the U.S. you know. And so I went up to talk to Benny, and he’d had a very hard head you know, and only money talked to Benny. And so he listened you know, and he pulled a long face. And I said, “We’re going to put on a…

926.t: Race and integration in Chicago music
926.s: Segregated locals and south/north side clubs, with music more integrated; Benny Goodman, Hampton and Billie Holiday cited as pioneers.
926.q: I guess so. It was a reflection of the times. Because at that time you had Local 208, which was the black local, and I’ve forgotten the name of the white Local, and then you had the south side and you had the north side. The south side was mostly black clubs, the north side was mostly white clubs.…

467.t: The Benny Goodman quartet and mixed audiences
467.s: Hampton joins Benny Goodman after Armstrong, in the first integrated group; he says audiences liked the soft sound and Teddy Wilson covered the bass with his left hand.
467.q: Yeah. Real big. And about the big band, you know I joined Benny Goodman after Louis Armstrong. And we were the first integrated group, the first black and white group.

165.t: Benny Goodman as a social hero in integrating his band
165.s: Goodman insisted on Hampton, Christian and Wilson despite business pressure; Hampton's gig and love of music.
165.q: Absolutely. Benny Goodman is an American social hero. He is a hero in the development of American society. Outside of music, Benny Goodman is a social hero. Because his love for the music was so pure that he just did not understand why he couldn’t have Lionel Hampton in his band, and then Charlie…

340.t: Benny Goodman, Sicilian prejudice and Grandpa Mancuso
340.s: On Goodman and Teddy Wilson, Mancuso links Sicilian experience of prejudice to jazz, and tells how his grandfather heckled his coach.
340.q: Yeah. Well I think that was part of the culture at the time you know. That’s all. But you know, he brazenly went ahead and he brought in Teddy Wilson. You know, it helped that John was pushing, Hammond was pushing him all the time. But he was a Jewish guy. So he understood it a little better. I…

584.t: Lionel Hampton on breaking racial barriers
584.s: Rowe relays Hampton's account of Teddy Wilson playing alone and of integrating the bandstand.
584.q: Yeah. Un hum. Yup. There you go.

422.t: Benny Goodman and integrating his organization
422.s: Pelote's reading-based take on why Goodman featured Wilson and Hampton as a side act, compared with Artie Shaw's approach.
422.ch: Henderson, Goodman and the swing era
422.q: Well my take on it is sort of what I’ve gotten from reading various books and articles. So I mean I wasn’t there so I can’t say I have any firsthand knowledge, but I just got the impression that, you know, he wanted these two musicians in his organization. He wanted Wilson and he wanted Hampton.…

548.t: Stanley Crouch, Lincoln Center and Benny Goodman's reputation
548.s: He doubts Lincoln Center's canon is racially neutral and defends Goodman as a color-barrier breaker; earlier greats succeeded despite segregation.
548.q: there, as much as they deny it. And I’ve sat down and I’ve talked to Stanley Crouch, I know Stanley Crouch, I know Wynton Marsalis a little bit, I mean we’ve talked a couple of times. I think I’ve talked more in depth with Stanley Crouch. And like he says that it’s not a racial thing, like we just…

444.t: Leadership qualities of bandleaders; Benny Goodman's treatment of Buddy Tate
444.s: Asked about leaders he admired or resented, Shew calls Goodman the most difficult and describes his racist treatment of Buddy Tate.
444.q: Yeah all of them had — I think the biggest idiot that I ever worked for and one of the most difficult people, and I’m not the only person who would tell you this, this has been written up in books, was Benny Goodman. He was an extremely difficult person, I think even his daughter I remember in an…

153.t: Comparing Goodman and Dorsey: swing bands and integration
153.s: He ranks Goodman among the real swing bands, notes Goodman's integrated band with Charlie Christian, and Dorsey's last-year interest in Basie-style writing by Ernie Wilkins.
153.ch: Contest, Goodman, the army and Tommy Dorsey
153.q: Quite different, but both great bands. To me, Benny Goodman joined ranks with Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Lionel Hampton, Cab Calloway, Jimmie Lunceford. Those were the real swing bands. Glenn Miller was a good band. Don’t get me wrong. He was the biggest moneymaker of all. But he wasn’t a swing…

86.t: Benny Goodman wanted Basie's rhythm section
86.s: Goodman tried to hire the Basie rhythm section and Lester Young, but hotels did not hire Black bands.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: You got that right, you know when you hit a bad one. But I would say, that was the greatest rhythm section that has ever been. In fact, Benny Goodman wanted to fire his whole rhythm section and hire the Basie rhythm section. It was around 1940 or something like that. He wanted Lester Young, he…

328.t: Woody Herman as progressive leader; Benny Goodman integrated band
328.s: Herman paid well, kept Blue Flame in the book while staying progressive; Goodman is praised for integration.
328.ch: Lloyd Price, Motown, Woody Herman and Europe
328.q: Woody was one of the best bandleaders I ever worked with. He paid the musicians a lot of respect. He paid them a lot of money, and still, at the same time, kept in mind what he had to do for the band to be popular. We played a lot of good music.

232.t: Why musicians revered Fields, and the white players Eli Wilinsky and Harold Iller
232.s: Love says every sideman respected him; Fields recalls a mixed band in 1928 before Benny Goodman, and Iller's chair.
232.q: He was very fine, and I enjoyed time with him, and the funniest thing about it, I think I told you when he first began, I had a white musician in twenty eight, and some say that Benny Goodman was the first to have a mixed band, but I had a mixed band in twenty eight--

91.s: Berger reads Mezzrow's account of a mixed band and a Carter arrangement; Carter does not remember it.
91.q: No, that's what I might call an interesting anecdote, but I don't remember it.

18.t: How Goodman became big; whites uptown
18.s: He says there was little white jazz downtown, so whites came uptown.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: Very little. You find jazz - that's why they came uptown. There was as many white people up here as there were Negros then. The Negros put them out.

388.t: No black musicians in Dorsey's band; Shavers and Teddy Wilson
388.s: Leeman says Charlie Shavers was the first black musician Dorsey hired, years after Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton joined Goodman, helped by John Hammond.
388.q: And then Benny saw that things were working out good, I think, giving credit where credit was due.

413.t: Debt to Goodman; Goodman's stand for Black players at the New Yorker
413.s: He owes his wife and son's path to Benny, and recounts Goodman refusing a hotel manager's demand that Black musicians use the kitchen.
413.q: That's how I met my wife, through Benny Goodman's band. My son picked his career through Benny Goodman's band. You know, with all the stories about Benny, I owe a great deal to him, really. He is a strange man but I always feel guilty when I say anything against him because I owe so much to him.
